Chapter 28

Live collaboration: a live query, a mailbox, and numbered operations

watchSheet is a query.live: an async generator that yields every time something happens on the sheet. Operations go the other way through a command, the server numbers them, and every tab applies the ones that are not its own echo.

By the end of this chapter

Build real-time collaboration on a live query with a broadcaster, a coalescing mailbox, and a clean exit when a browser goes away.

What travels is a batch: the operations one send carried, the version they produced, and the tab that sent them. A message is a list of batches, oldest first, plus who is in the room. The broadcaster is a Map of rooms, each a Map from listener to presence. join returns a leave function; broadcast sends one batch — or, given null, only the presence — to every listener; a cursor move updates one presence and broadcasts no batch at all. In-process, which is right for one server and would need a shared channel for two — the header says so.

The mailbox

Why the mailbox coalesces, and why it can be closed

Live streams are not event logs. If the sheet changes three times while a slow browser is still receiving the first message, it should get all three batches, in one message — so a push while nobody is waiting is appended to what is there. And close() exists because an async generator suspended on an await cannot be interrupted from outside: return() queues behind the pending promise, so a browser that closed its tab would keep its seat in the room until the next message happened to arrive. The end-to-end test that asserts Bob’s chip disappears when Bob leaves is the test that found this.

The generator: require a person who may open the sheet, join the room, and wire the request’s abort signal to the mailbox — the adapter fires it when the socket closes. Then catch up — every batch since the version the tab loaded — and loop on the mailbox until it is closed. The finally leaves the room, and it now runs promptly. Every id a tab sends is checked by one schema, ClientSchema, because it is now stored with each batch.

send applies a batch of operations to the stored document in a transaction with the op log, gets back the new version, and broadcasts the batch with its version and the sender’s client id. The sender receives its own batch and skips it; everyone else applies it.

The browser’s side

status is one value with four shapes, and only refused carries anything: the server’s own sentence. It is $state.raw because it is replaced, never changed inside — there is nothing in it for a deep proxy to watch — and the three plain shapes are single objects, so writing the state a tab is already in hands $state.raw the value it holds, which notifies nobody. The first version kept a status string and a separate problem, and nothing stopped the two disagreeing: the chip said “Saved” over a reason that no longer applied.

Why every batch carries its version, and the browser counts them

A browser can be handed the same batch twice, and there are three ways it happens. since is an argument of the live query, fixed when the page made it, so a reconnect after a dropped connection replays every batch since the page loaded. A new iterator — the page makes one after reconnect() — starts with the latest message, which the old loop may already have applied. And a batch committed between the room hearing about it and the catch-up being read is in both. Cells written twice come out the same; a row inserted twice is two rows, and every later edit lands one row out. The first version applied whatever arrived, and a probe that dropped the connection for half a second left the second tab showing a cell twice that the server held once. So each batch is taken in once, by version: anything at or below the version the page loaded is already in the sheet, and every later one is remembered in a set. A set, not a high-water mark, because two batches can arrive out of order and the earlier one must still be applied. The tab that sent a batch knows it by its client id — stored in the op log, so it survives the replay too — and skips it, because its own edits were applied as they were typed.

LiveSheet hooks the sheet’s onop: every local operation is queued, batched for a hundred milliseconds, and sent — a hundred at a time. What happens when a send fails depends on whether the server answered. A 4xx is the server refusing this batch — “A sheet may hold at most 200,000 cells”, a sheet that has been deleted, a session that has ended — and sending it again would be refused again, so the tab moves to refused with the server’s sentence and stops sending. Anything else — no answer at all, or a 5xx — may work in a moment, so the operations go back on the queue and it tries again in two seconds. Nothing is thrown: every caller is a timer or a navigation hook that would only turn a refusal into an unhandled rejection, and the outcome is status, which the page renders.

Why a refused sheet stops for good

When the server turns a batch down, the tab holds edits the stored sheet does not. Every operation after that is built on a sheet the server never saw: send it, and it may be accepted — a deleted cell, say — and the chip goes back to “Saved” over a sheet whose import is gone. That is what the first version did, and it is the worst thing a sheet can do: say it saved what it lost. So #enqueue refuses to queue anything once the status is refused, the edit stays on screen, and the page says what happened and offers the only honest way back: a reload, which builds the sheet again from what the server kept.

On the page, watchSheet(...) returns the live query, and the room’s operations are applied by iterating it. A live query is async-iterable, and the SvelteKit docs offer that for “direct, imperative access to the underlying stream of values (rather than the reactive current property)”. The first version applied messages in an effect that read current, which holds only the latest message: it saw each one only if Svelte happened to run the effect before the next arrived. The iterator has a rule too — “if values arrive faster than the consumer drains the iterator, only the latest pending value is kept” — so live.follow never keeps it waiting: receive is synchronous, and the loop asks for the next message in the same turn as it was handed the last, before the connection can deliver another. One loop lasts as long as the stream. A dropped connection does not end it — SvelteKit reconnects behind the same iterator, and the loop waits — so the effect starts a loop whenever the query is not done, and only a stream the server ended or refused needs a new one, which reconnect() brings. Starting the loop is wrapped in untrack. Subscribing reads the query’s latest value, and an effect depends on whatever it reads while it runs: without untrack, every message re-ran the effect, which threw its loop away and subscribed again — the new loop starting, as a new iterator does, with the message the old one had just applied. The version check absorbed the duplicates; untrack stops them being made. current and connected stay, for the status chip. beforeNavigate flushes the queue before the page is left, and the last effect’s cleanup disposes the connection.

The test for the replay: two tabs, a cell and then a row inserted above it, and the connection taken away and given back with setOffline. Against the first version it fails before the connection even drops: the second tab never shows the inserted row, because the effect reading current met a later message first. With the loop in place and the version check taken out, it fails after the reconnect instead — “first” pushed down a second row, because the catch-up applied the insert again. The refused batch has its own test in chapter 37, which imports more cells than the end-to-end server allows.

Checkpoint

  • You can say what happens when three operations arrive while a browser is slow, and how many messages it gets.
  • You can explain why return() on the generator was not enough and what the abort signal adds.
  • You can trace one keystroke from sheet.onop to another tab’s applyRemote.
  • You can name three ways a browser receives a batch it already has, and say what stops it applying one twice.
  • You can say which failures put operations back on the queue and which stop the tab, and why a refused tab does not resume.
